entries.b130f4e56102cf4c114ce099e732c8451e8e97c4: <div eID="gen24917" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24918" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24919" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24919" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24918" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24920" type="x-p"/> We must not despise correction. The prudent king. The flatterer. The just judge. Contend not with a fool. The prince who opens his ears to reports. The poor and the deceitful. The pious king. The insolent servant. The humiliation of the proud. Of the partner of a thief. The fear of man. The Lord the righteous Judge. <div eID="gen24920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24921" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24922" type="x-p"/> Hardeneth his neck - Becomes stubborn and obstinate.
entries.9418f9c1596935ff461e972246db90dc5afe8b1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24923" type="x-p"/> But he that keepeth company - רעה roeh, he that feedeth harlots, יאבד yeabed, shall utterly destroy his substance. Has there ever been a single case to the contrary?
entries.54ed9694f3a81347b3950e4864f22860a4414bc1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24924" type="x-p"/> He that receiveth gifts - This was notoriously the case in this kingdom, before the passing of the Magna Charta, or great charter of liberties. Hence that article in it, Nulli vendemus justitiam; "We will not sell justice to any." I have met with cases in our ancient records where, in order to get his right, a man was obliged almost to ruin himself in presents to the king, queen, and their favourites, to get the case decided in his favor.
entries.e53477ae6eb1daa70eb0f307cc1bd18869b0dc3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24925" type="x-p"/> Spreadeth a net for his feet - Beware of a flatterer; he does not flatter merely to please you, but to deceive you and profit himself.
entries.328b6e38fb88a0bdcceced2e507cc755f488d84e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24926" type="x-p"/> Whether he rage or laugh - Coverdale translates, "Yf a wyse man go to lawe with a foole, whether he deale with him frendly or roughly he geteth no rest."
entries.3b844017bc8c887ba612643b2bfff2696704dee6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24927" type="x-p"/> A fool uttereth all his mind - A man should be careful to keep his own secret, and never tell his whole mind upon any subject, while there are other opinions yet to be delivered; else, if he speak again, he must go over his old ground; and as he brings out nothing new, he injures his former argument.
entries.c29129f43e1a6c87de7bc88296dc997b75ef05f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24928" type="x-p"/> If a ruler hearken to lies - Wherever the system of espionage is permitted to prevail, there the system of falsity is established; for he who is capable of being a spy and informer, is not only capable of telling and swearing lies, but also of cutting his king's or even his father's throat. I have seen cases, where the same spy received pay from both parties, and deceived both.
entries.19d1bffd2a08f42e3502e6df349f4d3401f40d48: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24929" type="x-p"/> The poor and the deceitful man - It is difficult to fix the meaning of תככים techachim, which we here render the deceitful man. The Targum has, "The poor and the man of Little Wealth." The Septuagint, "The usurer and the Debtor." The Vulgate, "The poor and Creditor." Coverdale, "The poor and the Lender." Others, "The poor and the Rich;" "The poor and the Oppressors." I suppose the meaning may be the same as in <reference osisRef="Pro.22.2">Pro 22:2</reference> (note): "The rich and the poor meet together; the Lord is the Maker of them all." Where see the note.
entries.b56a2995b259194f8e16a212e298c7c7cbad7574: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24930" type="x-p"/> When the wicked are multiplied - That, in the multiplication of the wicked transgression is increased, requires no proof; but an important doctrine attaches to this. On this account wicked nations and wicked families are cut off and rooted out. Were it not so righteousness would in process of time be banished from the earth. This will account for many of the numerous instances in which whole families fail.
entries.1385a8e7dc2a0ecb43939cf5c842184ea8e00d96: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24931" type="x-p"/> Where there is no vision - My old MS. Bible, following the Vulgate, translates: Whan prophecye schal failen, the peple schal ben to scatered. Where Divine revelation, and the faithful preaching of the sacred testimonies, are neither reverenced nor attended, the ruin of that land is at no great distance. <div eID="gen24931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24932" type="x-p"/> But he that keepeth the law, happy is he - Go how it may with others, he shall be safe. So our Lord: "Blessed are they who hear the word of God, and keep it."
entries.7662e543cae70a9b48590b216edf089cae7a606b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24933" type="x-p"/> He that delicately bringeth up his servant - Such persons are generally forgetful of their obligations, assume the rights and privileges of children, and are seldom good for any thing.
entries.e9566b8ed67f6a9986583aad5e1814cf8dfa64f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24934" type="x-p"/> An angry man stirreth up strife - His spirit begets its like wherever he goes. <div eID="gen24934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24935" type="x-p"/> And a furious man aboundeth in transgression - His furious spirit is always carrying him into extremes, and each of these is a transgression.
entries.c355c283ee463439ee5b1a1dd54614dd9754c65d: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24936" type="x-p"/> A man's pride shall bring him low - A proud man is universally despised, and such are often exposed to great mortifications.
entries.1f76f9adadfa764f19943cecf347cbac96c779bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24937" type="x-p"/> Hateth his own soul - נפשו naphsho, his life, as the outraged law may at any time seize on and put him to death. <div eID="gen24937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24938" type="x-p"/> He heareth cursing - אלה alah, the execration or adjuration, (for all culprits were charged, as before God, to tell the truth), ולא יגד velo yagpid, but He will not tell It. He has no fear of God, nor reverence for an oath, because his heart is hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
entries.fb51e833312203e233f0578eb38b5a5f076bb247: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24939" type="x-p"/> The fear of man bringeth a snare - How often has this led weak men, though sincere in their general character, to deny their God, and abjure his people! See the case of Peter; and learn from this, O reader, that where the mighty have been slain, thou wilt fall, unless thou call on the Strong for strength, and for courage to use it. Be not ashamed of Jesus nor of his people, nor of his cross. Glory in this, that thou knowest him, art joined to them, and art counted worthy to bear it.
entries.e199e89c869160ff6548271b3124d36b9c3b01ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> Many seek the ruler's favor - To be screened from the punishment determined by the law; but should he grant the favor sought, and pardon the criminal, this takes not away his guilt in the sight of God, from whom all just judgment proceeds.
entries.4b9eedf442bf57bf6ca77de0ee2bef49f195e5bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> And he that is upright in the way - "But as for those that be in the right waye, the wicked hate them." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen24941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24942" type="x-p"/> To this verse the Vulgate adds the following: Verbum custodiens filius extra perditionem erit; "The son that keeps the word shall not fall into perdition." This is not in all copies of the Vulgate: but it was in that from which my old MS. Bible was made, where it is thus translated: The sone keping the worde schal ben out of perdicyon. I believe verbum here is intended for the Divine word; the revelation from God.  <chapter eID="Prov.29"/> <div eID="gen24942" type="x-p"/>

entries.f3ba100cdeaca56d3e4fa3a137f0c18cb2545bef: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.1">Pro 29:1</reference> <div eID="gen11864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11865" type="x-p"/> A general ethical proverb here follows: <div eID="gen11865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> A man often corrected who hardeneth his neck, <div eID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> Shall suddenly go to ruin without remedy. <div eID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> Line second = Pro 6:15. The connection אישׁ תּוכחות must make the nearest impression on a reader of the Book of Proverbs that they mean a censurer (reprehender), but which is set aside by what follows, for the genit. after אישׁ is, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.29">Pro 16:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.26.21">Pro 26:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference>, the designation of that which proceeds from the subject treated. And since תּוכחות, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.15">Psa 37:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.4">Job 23:4</reference>, denotes counter evidence, and generally rejoinders, thus in the first line a reasoner is designated who lets nothing be said to him, and nothing be shown to him, but contradicts all and every one. Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer: <hi type="italic">vir qui correptus contradicit et cervicem obdurat</hi>. But this interpolated <hi type="italic">correptus</hi> gives involuntary testimony of this, that the nearest lying impression of the 'אישׁ תו suffers a change by מקשׁה ערף: if we read הקשׁה (לב) ערף with 'תו, the latter then designates the correptio, over against which is placed obstinate boldness (Syr., Targ., Jerome, Luther), and 'תו shows itself thus to be <hi type="italic">gen. objecti</hi>, and we have to compare the gen. connection of אישׁ, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.23">Pro 18:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.17">Pro 21:17</reference>, or rather at 1Ki 20:42 and Jer 15:10. But it is unnecessary, with Hitzig, to limit 'תו to divine infliction of punishment, and after Hos 5:9; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.3">Isa 37:3</reference>, to read תוכחות [punishment], which occurs, <reference osisRef="Ps.149.7">Psa 149:7</reference>, in the sense of punishment inflicted by man.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Zunz, “Regarding the Idea and the Use of <hi type="italic">Tokhecha</hi>,” in Steinschneider’s <hi type="italic">Heb. Bibliographia</hi>, entitled המחכיר, 1871, p. 70f.</note> <div eID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> Besides, we must think first not of actual punishment, but of chastening, reproving words; and the man to whom are spoken the reproving words is one whose conduct merits more and more severe censure, and continually receives correction from those who are concerned for his welfare. Hitzig regards the first line as a conditional clause: “Is a man of punishment stiff-necked?”.... This is syntactically impossible. Only מקשׁה ערף could have such force: a man of punishment, if he.... But why then did not the author rather write the words והוא מקשׁה ערף? Why then could not מקשׁה ערף be a co-ordinated further description of the man? Cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ex. 17:21. The door of penitence, to which earnest, well-meant admonition calls a man, does not always remain open. He who with stiff-necked persistence in sin and in self-delusion sets himself in opposition to all endeavours to save his soul, shall one day suddenly, and without the prospect and possibility of restoration (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.19.11">Jer 19:11</reference>), become a wreck. <hi type="italic">Audi doctrinam si vis vitare ruinam</hi>.
entries.115fd554505c8cff5d3a2aa3883a85e8e969a599: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.2">Pro 29:2</reference> <div eID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> The general ethical proverb is here followed by one that is political: 2 When the righteous increase, the people rejoice;    And when a godless man ruleth, the people mourn. <div eID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> Regarding 'בּרבות צדּ (Aquila rightly, ἐν τῷ πληθῦναι δικαίους), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 28:28. If the righteous form the majority, or are in such numbers that they are the party that give the tone, that form the predominant power among the people (Fleischer, <hi type="italic">cum incrementa capiunt justi</hi>), then the condition of the people is a happy one, and their voice joyful (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.10">Pro 11:10</reference>); if, on the contrary, a godless man or (after <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Pro 28:1</reference>) godless men rule, the people are made to sigh (יאנח עם, with the <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>, according to rule). “There is reason,” as Hitzig remarks, “why עם should be placed first with, and then without, the article.” In the first case it denotes the people as those among whom there is such an increase of the righteous; in the second case, the article is wanting, because it is not generally used in poetry; and, besides, its absence makes the second line consist of nine syllables, like the first.
entries.cabbbd09a2e692f783dcb52be0ca7d55957e7df6: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.3">Pro 29:3</reference> <div eID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> This political proverb is now followed by one of general ethics: 3 A man who loveth wisdom delighteth his father;    And he who keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance. <div eID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of Pro 10:1. אישׁ־אהב has, according to rule, the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, cf. 9a. אישׁ is man, without distinction of age, from childhood (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.1">Gen 4:1</reference>) up to ripe old age (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.13">Isa 66:13</reference>); love and dutiful relation towards father and mother never cease. Line second reminds of <reference osisRef="Prov.28.7">Pro 28:7</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.20">Pro 13:20</reference>).
entries.e0b41c037cdcf72bb4f050469f8e29d86aeb6cec: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.4">Pro 29:4</reference> <div eID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> A series of six proverb follows, beginning with a proverb of the king: 4 A king by righteousness bringeth the land to a good condition;    But a man of taxes bringeth it down. <div eID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. חעמיד signifies to make it so that a person or matter comes to stand erect and stand fast (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 1Ki 15:4); הרס, to tear down, is the contrary of building up and extending (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>), cf. נהרס, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. רוּם, of the state, Pro 11:11. By 'אישׁ תּר is meant the king, or a man of this kind; but it is questionable whether as a man of gifts, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, one who lets gifts be made to him (Grotius, Fleischer, Ewald, Bertheau, Zöckler), or as a man of taxes, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who imposes them (Midrash, Aben Ezra, Ralbag, Rosenmüller, Hitzig). Both interpretations are possible, for 'תר means tax (lifting, raising = dedicating), free-will offerings, as well as gifts that are obligatory and required by the laws of nature. Since the word, in the only other place where it occurs, <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.13-Ezek.45.16">Eze 45:13-16</reference>, is used of the relation of the people to the prince, and denotes a legally-imposed tax, so it appears also here, in passing over from the religious sphere to the secular, to be meant of taxes, and that according to its fundamental conception of gifts, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, such taxes as are given on account of anything, such as the produce of the soil, manufactures, heritages. Thus also is to be understood Aquila’s and Theodotion’s ἀνὴρ ἀφαιρεμάτων, and the rendering also of the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἐράνων. A man on the throne, covetous of such gifts, brings the land to ruin by exacting contributions; on the contrary, a king helps the land to a good position, and an enduring prosperity, by the exercise of right, and that in appointing a well-proportioned and fit measure of taxation.
entries.fc79c76fcb0b501c3103570faed375724dc2b1bb: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.5">Pro 29:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.5">5</reference> A man who flattereth his neighbour    Spreadeth a net for his steps. <div eID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> Fleischer, as Bertheau: <hi type="italic">vir qui alterum blanditiis circumvenit</hi>; but in the על there does not lie in itself a hostile tendency, an intention to do injury; it interchanges with אל, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.3">Psa 36:3</reference>, and what is expressed in line second happens also, without any intention on the part of the flatterer: the web of the flatterer before the eyes of a neighbour becomes, if he is caught thereby, a net for him in which he is entangled to his own destruction (Hitzig). החליק signifies also, without any external object, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.23">Pro 28:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.2.16">Pro 2:16</reference>, as internally transitive: to utter that which is smooth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, flattering. פּעמיו is, as <reference osisRef="Ps.57.7">Psa 57:7</reference> = רגליו, for which it is the usual Phoenician word.
entries.c76e4595aacf652366b573ad115fbc1cc6af5133: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">Pro 29:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.6">6</reference> In the transgression of the wicked man lies a snare;    But the righteous rejoiceth jubelt and is glad. <div eID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> Thus the first line is to be translated according to the sequence of the accents, <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, for the second <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> is the transformation of Dechi; אישׁ רע thus, like אנשׁי־רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.5">Pro 28:5</reference>, go together, although the connection is not, like this, genitival, but adjectival. But there is also this sequence of the accents, <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi>, <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, which separates רע and אישׁ. According to this, Ewald translates: “in the transgression of one lies an evil snare;” but in that case the word ought to have been מוקשׁ רע, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference>; for although the numeral רבים sometimes precedes its substantive, yet no other adjective ever does; passages such as <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.30">Isa 10:30</reference> do not show the possibility of this position of the words. In this sequence of accents the explanation must be: in the wickedness of a man is the evil of a snare, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, evil is the snare laid therein (Böttcher); but a reason why the author did not write מוקשׁ רע would also not be seen there, and thus we must abide by the accentuation אישׁ רע. The righteous also may fall, yet he is again raised by means of repentance and pardon; but in the wickedness of a bad man lies a snare into which having once fallen, he cannot again release himself from it, Pro 24:16. In the second line, the form ירוּן, for ירן, is defended by the same metaplastic forms as ישׁוּד, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.6">Psa 91:6</reference>; ירוּץ, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa 42:4</reference>; and also that the order of the words is not ישׂמח ורנּן (lxx ἐν χαρᾷ καὶ ἐν εὐθροσύνῃ; Luther: <hi type="italic">frewet sich und hat wonne</hi> [rejoices and has pleasure]), is supported by the same sequence of ideas, Zec 2:1-13 :14, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.31.7">Jer 31:7</reference> : the <hi type="italic">Jubeln</hi> is the momentary outburst of gladness; the <hi type="italic">Freude</hi> gladness, however, is a continuous feeling of happiness. To the question as to what the righteous rejoiceth over [<hi type="italic">jubelt</hi>] and is glad [<hi type="italic">greuet</hi>] because of, the answer is not: because of his happy release from danger (Zöckler), but: because of the prosperity which his virtue procures for him (Fleischer). But the contrast between the first and second lines is not clear and strong. One misses the expression of the object or ground of the joy. Cocceius introduces into the second line a <hi type="italic">si lapsus fuerit</hi>. Schultens translates, <hi type="italic">justus vel succumbens triumphabit</hi>, after the Arab. rân f. o., which, however, does not mean <hi type="italic">succumbere</hi>, but <hi type="italic">subigere</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.78.65">Psa 78:65</reference>). Hitzig compares Arab. raym f. i., <hi type="italic">discedere, relinquere</hi>, and translates: “but the righteous passeth through and rejoiceth.” Böttcher is inclined to read יראה ושׂמח, he sees it (what?) and rejoiceth. All these devices, however, stand in the background compared with Pinsker’s proposal (<hi type="italic">Babylon.-Heb. Punktationssystem</hi>, p. 156): “On the footsteps of the wicked man lie snares, <div eID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> But the righteous runneth and is glad,”<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he runneth joyfully (like the sun, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">Psa 19:6</reference>) on the divinely-appointed way (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.132">Psa 119:132</reference>), on which he knows himself threatened by no danger. The change of בפשׁע into בפשׂע has <reference osisRef="Prov.12.13">Pro 12:13</reference> against it; but ירוץ may be regarded, after <reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">Pro 4:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Pro 18:10</reference>, as the original from which ירון is corrupted.
entries.1df5f6d1c0b39cf7381d416c7e1e624ddad07b62: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.7">Pro 29:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.7">7</reference> The righteous knoweth the cause of the poor,    But the godless understandeth no knowledge. <div eID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11879" type="x-p"/> The righteous knoweth and recogniseth the righteous claims of people of low estate, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, what is due to them as men, and in particular cases; but the godless has no knowledge from which such recognition may go forth (cf. as to the expression, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.25">Pro 19:25</reference>). The proverb begins like <reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">Pro 12:10</reference>, which commends the just man’s compassion to his cattle; this commends his sympathy with those who are often treated as cattle, and worse even than cattle. The lxx translates 7b twice: the second time reading רשׁ instead of רשׁע, it makes nonsense of it.
entries.f06e61e136342df2b0c475521de7f22857c7c2c1: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.8">Pro 29:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.8">8</reference> Men of derision set the city in an uproar,    But wise men allay anger. <div eID="gen11879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11880" type="x-p"/> Isa. 28 shows what we are to understand by אנשׁי לצון: men to whom nothing is holy, and who despise all authority. The <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> יפיחוּ does not signify <hi type="italic">irretiunt</hi>, from פּחח (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. παγιδιοῦσι, after Kimchi, Aben Ezra, and others), but <hi type="italic">sufflant</hi>, from פוח (Rashi: ילהיבו): they stir up or excite the city, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, its inhabitants, so that they begin to burn as with flames, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by the dissolution of the bonds of mutual respect and of piety, by the letting loose of passion, they disturb the peace and excite the classes of the community and individuals against each other; but the wise bring it about that the breathings of anger that has broken forth, or is in the act of breaking forth, are allayed. The anger is not that of God, as it is rendered by Jerome and Luther, and as יפיחו freely translated might mean. The Aram. err in regard to יפיחו in passages such as Pro 6:19.
entries.83531426be14e52c5694b4abe93c322e858e4abe: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.9">Pro 29:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.9">9</reference> If a wise man has to contend with a fool,    He the fool rageth and laugheth, and hath no rest. <div eID="gen11880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11881" type="x-p"/> Among the old translators, Jerome and Luther take the “wise man” as subject even of the second line, and that in all its three members: <hi type="italic">vir sapiens si cum stulto contenderit, sive irascatur sive reideat, non inveniet requiem</hi>. Thus Schultens, C. B. Michaelis, Umbreit, Ewald, Elster, and also Fleischer: “The doubled <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> is correlative, as at <reference osisRef="Exod.21.16">Exo 21:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.5.3">Lev 5:3</reference>, and expresses the perfect sameness in respect of the effect, here of the want of effect. If the wise man, when he disputes with a fool, becomes angry, or jests, he will have no rest, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he will never bring it to pass that the fool shall cease to reply; he yields the right to him, and thus makes it possible for him to end the strife.” But the angry passion, and the bursts of laughter alternating therewith, are not appropriate to the wise man affirming his right; and since, after <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.17">Ecc 9:17</reference>, the words of the wise are heard בּנחח, the ואין נחת [and there is no rest] will cause us to think of the fool as the logical subject. So far correctly, but in other respects inappropriately, the lxx ἀνὴρ σοφὸς κρινεῖ ἔθνη (after the expression עם, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, עם, instead of את), ἀνὴρ δὲ φαῦλος (which אישׁ אויל does not mean) ὀργιζόμενος καταγελᾶται καὶ οὐ καταπτήσσει (as if the words were ולא יחת).<note placement="foot">According to this the Targum ולא מתתּבר (he remains obstinate), according to which the ולא מתתפיר (he does not lose his wits) of the Peshito is perhaps to be corrected. The distribution of the subjects is obscure.</note> <div eID="gen11881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11882" type="x-p"/> The syntactical relation would be simpler if נשׁפּט in 9a were vocalized as a hypothetical perfect. But we read for it the past נשׁפּט. Ewald designates 9a as a conditional clause, and Hitzig remarks that the Lat. <hi type="italic">viro sapiente disceptante cum stulto</hi> corresponds therewith. It marks, like <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.13">1Sa 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>, the situation from which there is a departure then with <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>.: if a wise man in the right is in contact with a fool, he starts up, and laughs, and keeps not quiet (supply לּו as at <reference osisRef="Prov.28.27">Pro 28:27</reference>), or (without לו): there is no keeping quiet, there is no rest. The figure is in accordance with experience. If a wise man has any controversy with a fool, which is to be decided by reasonable and moral arguments, then he becomes boisterous and laughs, and shows himself incapable of quietly listening to his opponent, and of appreciating his arguments.
entries.7e4881a1409e7667b0f8904fa12974d3992aee41: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference> <div eID="gen11882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11883" type="x-p"/> We now group together <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference>-14. Of these, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.29.11">Pro 29:11</reference> are alike in respect of the tense used; <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12-Prov.29.14">Pro 29:12-14</reference> have in common the pronoun pointing back to the first member. 10 Men of blood hate the guiltless      And the upright; they attempt the life of such <div eID="gen11883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11884" type="x-p"/> The nearest lying translation of the second line would certainly be: the upright seek his soul (that of the guiltless). In accordance with the contrasted ישׂנאו, the Aram. understand the seeking of earnest benevolent seeking, but disregarding the נפשׁ in לנפשׁו;<note placement="foot">The Targum translates תם, guiltlessness, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. (μισοῦσι) γνῶσιν, turning to Pro 1:22.</note> <div eID="gen11884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11885" type="x-p"/> Symmachus (ἐπιζητήσουσι), Jerome (<hi type="italic">quaerunt</hi>), and Luther thus also understand the sentence; and Rashi remarks that the phrase is here לשׁון חבּה, for he rests; but mistrusting himself, refers to <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.15">1Sa 21:1-15</reference> :23. Ahron b. Josef glosses: to enter into friendship with him. Thus, on account of the contrast, most moderns, interpreting the phrase <hi type="italic">sensu bono</hi>, also Fleischer: <hi type="italic">probi autem vitam ejus conservare student</hi>. The thought is, as <reference osisRef="Prov.12.6">Pro 12:6</reference> shows, correct; but the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>. protests against this rendering, which can rest only on <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">Psa 142:5</reference>, where, however, the poet does not say אין דּורשׁ נפשׁי, but, as here also the <hi type="italic">usus loq</hi>. requires, לנפשׁי. There are only three possible explanations which Aben Ezra enumerates: (1) they seek his, the bloody man’s, soul, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, they attempt his life, to take vengeance against him, according to the meaning of the expressions as generally elsewhere, used, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>; (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.2">2</reference>) they revenge his, the guiltless man’s, life (lxx ἐκζητήσουσιν), which has fallen a victim, after the meaning in which elsewhere only בּקּשׁ דּם and דּרשׁ נפשׁ, <reference osisRef="Gen.9.5">Gen 9:5</reference>, occur. This second meaning also is thus not in accordance with the usage of the words, and against both meanings it is to be said that it is not in the spirit of the Book of Proverbs to think of the ישׁרים [the upright, righteous] as executors of the sentences of the penal judicature. There thus remains<note placement="foot">For εὐθεῖς δὲ συνάξουσιν (will bring away?) τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτῶν, understood after <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer 45:5</reference>, lies linguistically yet further off.</note> the interpretation (3): the upright - they (the bloody men) seek the soul of such an one. The transition from the plur. to the sing. is individualizing, and thus the arrangement of the words is like <reference osisRef="Gen.47.21">Gen 47:21</reference> : “And the people (as regards them), he removed them to the cities,” Gesen. §145. 2. This last explanation recommends itself by the consideration that תם and ישׁרים are cognate as to the ideas they represents-let one call to mind the common expression תּם וישׁר [perfect and upright, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.1.1">Job 1:1</reference>; Job 2:3], - that the same persons are meant thereby, and it is rendered necessary by this, that the thought, “bloody men hate the guiltless,” is incomplete; for the same thing may also be said of the godless in general. One expects to hear that just against the guiltless, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, men walking in their innocence, the bloody-mindedness of such men is specially directed, and 10b says the same thing; this second clause first brings the contrast to the point aimed at. Lutz is right in seeking to confute Hitzig, but he does so on striking grounds.
entries.9195298ccabbb39921d5dcadadcf8270a362d8f1: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.11">Pro 29:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.11">11</reference> All his wrath the fool poureth out;      But the wise man husheth it up in the background. <div eID="gen11885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11886" type="x-p"/> That רוּחו is not meant here of his spirit (Luther) in the sense of <hi type="italic">quaecunque in mente habet</hi> (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Fleischer) the contrast shows, for ישׁבּחנּה does not signify <hi type="italic">cohibet</hi>, for which יחשׁכנּה (lxx ταμιεύεται) would be the proper word: רוּח thus is not here used of passionate emotion, such as at <reference osisRef="Prov.16.31">Pro 16:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">Isa 25:4</reference>; Isa 33:11. שׁבּח is not here equivalent to Arab. sabbah, αἰνεῖν (Imman., <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Heidenheim), which does not supply an admissible sense, but is equivalent to Arab. sabbakh, to quiet (Ahron b. Josef: קטפיאון = καταπαύειν), the former going back to the root-idea of extending (<hi type="italic">amplificare</hi>), the latter to that of going to a distance, putting away: sabbakh, <hi type="italic">procul recessit, distitit</hi>, hence שׁבּח, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.10">Psa 89:10</reference>, and here properly to drive off into the background, synon. השׁיב (Fleischer). But בּאחור (only here with ב) is ambiguous. One might with Rashi explain: but the wise man finally, or afterwards (Symmachus, ἐπ ̓ ἐσχάτων; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. κατόπιν = κατόπισθε), appeaseth the anger which the fool lets loose; <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, if the latter gives vent to his anger, the former appeases, subdues, mitigates it (cf. בּאחרנה, לאחור, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.23">Isa 42:23</reference>). But it lies still nearer to refer the antithesis to the anger of the wise man himself; he does not give to it unbridled course, but husheth it in the background, viz., in his heart. Thus Syr. and Targ. reading בּרעינא, the former, besides יחשּׁבנּה (<hi type="italic">reputat eam</hi>), so also Aben Ezra: in the heart as the background of the organ of speech. Others explain: in the background, afterward, <hi type="italic">retrorsum</hi>, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Nolde, but to which <hi type="italic">compescit</hi> would be more appropriate than <hi type="italic">sedat</hi>. Hitzig’s objection, that in other cases the expression would be בּקרבּו, is answered by this, that with באחור the idea of pressing back (of אחוּר) is connected. The order of the words also is in favour of the meaning <hi type="italic">in recessu</hi> (<hi type="italic">cordis</hi>). <hi type="italic">Irae dilatio mentis pacatio</hi> (according to an old proverb).
entries.1f2c82a0f9c6c7b125e40bf5fdbbeccbdc24454d: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Pro 29:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">12</reference> A ruler who listens to deceitful words,      All his servants are godless. <div eID="gen11886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11887" type="x-p"/> They are so because they deceive him, and they become so; for instead of saying the truth which the ruler does not wish to hear, they seek to gain his favour by deceitful flatteries, misrepresentations, exaggerations, falsehoods. <hi type="italic">Audita rex quae praecipit lex</hi>. He does not do this, as the saying is, <hi type="italic">sicut rex ita grex</hi> (Sir. 10:2), in the sense of this proverb of Solomon.
entries.ffe39df8c2e19f33a3a9c893f2a4005222631086: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.13">Pro 29:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.13">13</reference> The poor man and the usurer meet together -      Jahve lighteneth the eyes of both. <div eID="gen11887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11888" type="x-p"/> A variation of <reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">Pro 22:2</reference>, according to which the proverb is to be understood in both of its parts. That אישׁ תּככים is the contrast of רשׁ, is rightly supposed in <hi type="italic">Temura</hi> 16b; but Rashi, who brings out here a man of moderate learning, and Saadia, a man of a moderate condition (thus also the Targ. גּברא מצעיא, after Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">homo mediocris fortunae</hi>), err by connecting the word with תּוך. The lxx δανειστοῦ καὶ χρεωφειλέτου (ἀλλήλοις συνελθόντων), which would be more correct inverted, for אישׁ תככים is a man who makes oppressive taxes, high previous payments of interest; the verbal stem תּכך, Arab. tak, is a secondary to R. wak, which has the meanings of pressing together, and pressing firm (whence also the middle is named; cf. Arab. samym âlaklab, the solid = the middle point of the heart). תּך, with the plur. תככים, scarcely in itself denotes interest, τόκος; the designation אישׁ תככים includes in it a sensible reproach (Syr. afflictor), and a <hi type="italic">rentier</hi> cannot be so called (Hitzig). Luther: <hi type="italic">Reiche</hi> [rich men], with the marginal note: “who can practise usury as they then generally all do?” Therefore Löwenstein understands the second line after <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.7">1Sa 2:7</reference> : God enlighteneth their eyes by raising the lowly and humbling the proud. But this line, after <reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">Pro 22:2</reference>, only means that the poor as well as the rich owe the light of life (<reference osisRef="Ps.13.4">Psa 13:4</reference>) to God, the creator and ruler of all things - a fact which has also its moral side: both are conditioned by Him, stand under His control, and have to give to Him an account; or otherwise rendered: God maketh His sun to rise on the low and the high, the evil and the good (cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mat 5:45</reference>) - an all-embracing love full of typical moral motive.<note placement="foot">מאיר has, by Löwenstein, <hi type="italic">Mehuppach Legarmeh</hi>, but incorrectly, since after <hi type="italic">Legarmeh</hi> two conjunctives cannot occur. Also Norzi with <hi type="italic">Mehuppach</hi> <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> is irregular, since Ben-Asher recognises only two examples of this double accentuation to which this מאיר does not belong; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 12. That the <hi type="italic">penultima</hi> toning מאיר in several editions is false scarcely needs to be remarked. Jablonski rightly points with <hi type="italic">Mehuppach</hi> on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>., and <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi> on the preceding open syllable.</note>
entries.379ddc41a01188c5df8d22315264b79aab2ff3a4: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.14">Pro 29:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.14">14</reference> A king who judgeth the poor with truth,      His throne shall stand for ever. בּאמת, as at <reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Isa 16:5</reference> (synon. באמונה, במישׁרים, במישׁור), is equivalent to fidelity to duty, or a complete, full accomplishment of his duty as a ruler with reference to the dispensing of justice; in other words: after the norm of actual fact, and of the law, and of his duty proceeding from both together. מלך has in Codd., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>., and in the Venetian 1517, 21, rightly <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>. In that which follows, שׁופט באמת are more closely related than באמת דלים, for of two conjunctives standing together the first always connects more than the second. מלך שׁופט באמת דלים is the truest representation of the logical grammatical relation. To 14b compare the proverb of the king, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.12">Pro 16:12</reference>; Pro 25:5.
entries.15bc73d1d5276d42b3b3fff1b166bc94c3fc0783: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.15">Pro 29:15</reference> <div eID="gen11888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11889" type="x-p"/> A proverb with שׁבט, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.15">Pro 29:15</reference>, is placed next to one with שׁופט, but it begins a group of proverbs regarding discipline in the house and among the people: 15 The rod and reproof give wisdom;      But an undisciplined son is a shame to his mother. <div eID="gen11889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11890" type="x-p"/> With שׁבט [a rod], which <reference osisRef="Prov.22.15">Pro 22:15</reference> also commends as salutary, תּוכחת refers to discipline by means of words, which must accompany bodily discipline, and without them is also necessary; the construction of the first line follows in number and gender the scheme <reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pro 27:9</reference>, Zec 7:7; Ewald, §339c. In the second line the mother is named, whose tender love often degenerates into a fond indulgence; such a darling, such a mother’s son, becomes a disgrace to his mother. Our “<hi type="italic">ausgelassen</hi>,” by which Hitzig translates משׁלּח, is used of joyfulness unbridled and without self-restraint, and is in the passage before us too feeble a word; שׁלּח is used of animals pasturing at liberty, wandering in freedom (<reference osisRef="Job.39.5">Job 39:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Isa 16:2</reference>); נער משׁלח is accordingly a child who is kept in by no restraint and no punishment, one left to himself, and thus undisciplined (Luther, Gesenius, Fleischer, and others).
entries.1a3c20349d07946af0c45da64e3d3b99ccccc777: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.16">Pro 29:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.16">16</reference> When the godless increase, wickedness increaseth;      But the righteous shall see their fall. <div eID="gen11890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11891" type="x-p"/> The lxx translation is not bad: πολλῶν ὄντων ἀσεβῶν πολλαὶ γίνονται ἁμαρτίαι (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding רבה, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.2">Pro 29:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.28">Pro 28:28</reference>); but in the main it is only a <hi type="italic">Binsenwahrheit</hi>, as they say in Swabia, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a trivial saying. The proverb means, that if among a people the party of the godless increases in number, and at the same time in power, wickedness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a falling away into sins of thought and conduct, and therewith wickedness, prevails. When irreligion and the destruction of morals thus increase, the righteous are troubled; but the conduct of the godless carries the judgment in itself, and the righteous shall with joy perceive, in the righteous retribution of God, that the godless man will be cast down from his power and influence. This proverb is like a motto to <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1">Psa 12:1</reference>-8.
entries.3338362c5a2d6a075d2ff10a41c21f849348fe98: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.17">Pro 29:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.17">17</reference> Correct thy son, and he will give thee delight,      And afford pleasure to thy soul. <div eID="gen11891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11892" type="x-p"/> The lxx well translates ויניחך by καὶ ἀναπαύσει σε;<note placement="foot">Their translation of <reference osisRef="Prov.29.17">Pro 29:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.29.18">Pro 29:18</reference> here is found, in a marred and mutilated form, after Pro 28:17. At that place the words are καὶ ἀγαπήσει σε.</note> הניח denotes rest properly, a breathing again, ἀνάψυξις; and then, with an obliteration of the idea of restraint so far, generally (like the Arab. araḥ, compared by Fleischer) to afford pleasure or delight. The post.-bibl. language uses for this the words נחת רוּח, and says of the pious that he makes נחת רוח to his Creator, <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 17a; and of God, that He grants the same to them that fear Him, <hi type="italic">Berach</hi>. 29b; in the morning prayer of the heavenly spirits, that they hallow their Creator בנחת רוח (with inward delight). Write with Codd. (also <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>.) and older editions ויניחך, not ויניחךּ; for, except in verbs 'ה'ל, the suffix of this <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form is not dageshed, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, אמיתך, 1Ki 2:26; cf. also 1Ki 22:16 and Psa 50:8. מעדנּים the lxx understands, after <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.24">2Sa 1:24</reference> (עם־עדנים, μετὰ κόσμου), also here, of ornament; but the word signifies dainty dishes - here, high spiritual enjoyment. As in <reference osisRef="Prov.29.15">Pro 29:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.29.16">Pro 29:16</reference> a transition was made from the house to the people, so there now follows the proverb of the discipline of children, a proverb of the education of the people:
entries.29c326e4b548e04a1202d75c37ce64b61cd74aa6: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.18">Pro 29:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.18">18</reference> Without a revelation a people becomes ungovernable;      But he that keepeth the law, happy is he. <div eID="gen11892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11893" type="x-p"/> Regarding the importance of this proverb for estimating the relation of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> to prophecy, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., vol. i. p. 41. חזון is, according to the sense, equivalent to נבוּאה, the prophetic revelation in itself, and as the contents of that which is proclaimed. Without spiritual preaching, proceeding from spiritual experience, a people is unrestrained (יפּרע, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the punctuation at <reference osisRef="Prov.28.25">Pro 28:25</reference>, and regarding the fundamental meaning, at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.25">Pro 1:25</reference>); it becomes פּרע, disorderly, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.25">Exo 32:25</reference>; <hi type="italic">wild und wüst</hi>, as Luther translates. But in the second line, according to the unity of the antithesis, the words are spoken of the people, not of individuals. It is therefore not to be explained, with Hitzig: but whoever, in such a time, nevertheless holds to the law, it is well with him! Without doubt this proverb was coined at a time when the preaching of the prophets was in vogue; and therefore this, “but whoever, notwithstanding,” is untenable; such a thought at that time could not at all arise; and besides this, תורה is in the Book of Proverbs a moveable conception, which is covered at least by the law in contradistinction to prophecy. Tôra denotes divine teaching, the word of God; whether that of the Sinaitic or that of the prophetic law (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>). While, on the one hand, a people is in a dissolute condition when the voice of the preacher, speaking from divine revelation, and enlightening their actions and sufferings by God’s word, is silent amongst them (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Psa 74:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.8.12">Amo 8:12</reference>); on the other hand, that same people are to be praised as happy when they show due reverence and fidelity to the word of God, both as written and as preached. That the word of God is preached among a people belongs to their condition of life; and they are only truly happy when they earnestly and willingly subordinate themselves to the word of God which they possess and have the opportunity of hearing. אשׁרהוּ (defective for אשׁריהוּ) is the older, and here the poetic kindred form to אשׁריו, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.21">Pro 14:21</reference>; Pro 16:20.
entries.3dc0a1eb0ee6daf9d207a68741a5d7344517ca53: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.19">Pro 29:19</reference> <div eID="gen11893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11894" type="x-p"/> From the discipline of the people this series of proverbs again returns to the discipline of home: 19 With words a servant will not let himself be bettered;      For he understandeth them, but conformeth not thereto. <div eID="gen11894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11895" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נוסר becomes a so-called tolerative, for it connects with the idea of happening that of reaching its object: to become truly bettered (taught in wisdom, corrected), and thus to let himself be bettered. With mere words this is not reached; the unreasonable servant needs, in order to be set right, a more radical means of deliverance. This assertion demands confirmation; therefore is the view of von Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Schriftbew</hi>. ii. 2. 404) improbable, that 19b has in view a better-disposed servant: supposing that he is intelligent, in which case he is admonished without cause, then the words are also lost: he will let them pass over him in silence without any reply. This attempted explanation is occasioned by this, that מענה can signify nothing else than a response in words. If this were correct, then without doubt its fundamental meaning would correspond with כּי; for one explains, with Löwenstein, “for he perceives it, and may not answer,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, this, that a reply cut off frustrates the moral impression. Or also: for he understands it, but is silent - <hi type="italic">in praefractum se silentium configit</hi> (Schultens); and thus it is with the ancients (Rashi). But why should not ואין מענה itself be the expression of this want of any consequences? מענה cannot certainly mean humiliation<note placement="foot">The Syr. and Targ. also think on ענה, for they translate: “for he knows that he receives no strokes.”</note> (Meîri, after <reference osisRef="Exod.10.3">Exo 10:3</reference>, הכנעה), but why as an answer in words and not also a response by act (Stuart: a practical answer)? Thus the lxx ἐὰν γὰρ καὶ νοήσῃ, ἀλλ ̓ οὐχ ὑπακούσεται, according to which Luther: for although he at once understands it, he does not yet take it to himself. That מענה tahT . may mean obedience, the Aram. so understood, also at Pro 16:4. It denoted a reply in the most comprehensive meaning of the word, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 16:1. The thought, besides, is the same as if one were to explain: for he understands it, and is silent, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, lets thee speak; or: he understands it, but that which he perceives finds no practical echo.
entries.b7f89cb3585b3f6ddb3b206269ac503ce8484d4a: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.20">Pro 29:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.20">20</reference> Seest thou a man hasty in his words?      The fool hath more hope than he. <div eID="gen11895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11896" type="x-p"/> Cf. Pro 26:12. Such an one has blocked up against himself the path to wisdom, which to the fool, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to the ingenuous, stands open; the former is perfect, of the latter something may yet be made. In this passage the contrast is yet more precise, for the fool is thought of as the dull, which is the proper meaning of כּסיל, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Pro 17:24. There is more hope for the fool than for him, although he may be no fool in himself, who overthrows himself by his words. “The προπετὴς ἐν λόγῳ αὐτοῦ (Sir. 9:18) has, in the existing case, already overleaped the thought; the כסיל has it still before him, and comes at length, perhaps with his slow conception, to it” (Hitzig); for the ass, according to the fable, comes at last farther than the greyhound. Hence, in words as well as in acts, the proverb holds good, “<hi type="italic">Eile mit Weile</hi>” [= <hi type="italic">festina lente</hi>]. Every word, as well as act, can only be matured by being thought out, and thought over. From this proverb, which finds its practical application to the affairs of a house, and particularly also to the relation to domestics, the group returns to the subject of instruction, which is its ground-tone.
entries.0135b3899ad21a35f9062d309632197ea030b230: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.21">Pro 29:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.21">21</reference> If one pampers his servant from youth up,      He will finally reach the place of a child. <div eID="gen11896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11897" type="x-p"/> The lxx had no answer to the question as to the meaning of מנון. On the other hand, for פּנּק, the meaning to fondle; <hi type="italic">delicatius enutrire</hi>, is perfectly warranted by the Aram. and Arab. The Talmud, <hi type="italic">Succa</hi> 52b, resorts to the alphabet בח''אט in order to reach a meaning for מנון. How the Targ. comes to translate the word by מנסּח (outrooted) is not clear; the rendering of Jerome: <hi type="italic">postea sentiet eum contumacem</hi>, is perhaps mediated by the ἔσται γογγυσμός of Symmachus, who combines נון with לון, <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. γογγύζειν. The ὀθυνηθήσεται of the lxx, with the Syr., von Hofmann has sought to justify (<hi type="italic">Schriftbew</hi>. ii. 2. 404), for he derives מנון = מנהון from נהה. We must then punctuate מנּון; but perhaps the lxx derived the word from אנן = מאנון, whether they pronounced it מנון (cf. מסרת = מאסרת) or מנּון. To follow them is not wise, for the formation of the word is precarious; one does not see with the speaker of this proverb, to whom the language presented a fulness of synonyms for the idea of complaint, meant by using this peculiar word. Linguistically these meanings are impossible: of Jerome, <hi type="italic">dominus</hi> = ממנּה (Ahron b. Josef, Meîri, and others); or: the oppressed = מוּנה, from ינה (Johlson); or: one who is sick = מונה (Euchel). and Ewald’s “<hi type="italic">undankbar</hi>” [unthankful], derived from the Arabic, is a mere fancy, since (Arab.) manuwan does not mean one who is unthankful, but, on the contrary, one who upbraids good deeds shown.<note placement="foot">In <hi type="italic">Jahrb</hi>. xi. p. 10f. Ewald compares, in an expressive way, the Ethiopic mannána (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi>) to scorn; menûn, a reprobate; and mannânı̂, one who is despised; according to which מנון hcih could certainly designate “a man despising scornfully his own benefactors, or an unthankful man.” But this verbal stem is peculiarly Ethiop., and is certainly not once found in Arab. For minnat (which Ewald compares) denotes benefaction, and the duty laid on one thereby, the dependence thereby produced. The verb (Arab.) minn (= מנן) signifies to divide; and particularly, partly to confer benefaction, partly to attribute benefaction, reckon to, enumerate, and thereby to bring out the sense of obligation. Thus nothing is to be derived from this verbal stem for מנון.</note> <div eID="gen11897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11898" type="x-p"/> The ancients are in the right track, who explain מנון after the verb נוּן, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Psa 72:17</reference> = נין = בּן; the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., herein following Kimchi, also adopts the nominal form, for it translates (but without perceptible meaning) γόνωσις. Luther’s translation is fortunate: “If a servant is tenderly treated from youth up, <div eID="gen11898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11899" type="x-p"/> He will accordingly become a <hi type="italic">Junker</hi> [squire].” <div eID="gen11899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11900" type="x-p"/> The ideas represented in modern Jewish translations: that of a son (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Solomon: he will at last be the son) and that of a master (Zunz), are here united. But how the idea of a son (from the verb נון), at the same time that of a master, may arise, is not to be perceived in the same way as with <hi type="italic">Junker</hi> and the Spanish <hi type="italic">infante</hi> and <hi type="italic">hidalgo</hi>; rather with מנון, as the ironical naming of the son (little son), the idea of a weakling (de Wette) may be connected. The state of the matter appears as follows: - the Verb נוּן has the meanings of luxuriant growth, numerous propagation; the fish has from this the Aram. name of נוּן, like the Heb. דּג, from דּגה, which also means luxuriant, exuberant increase (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Psa 72:17</reference>). From this is derived נין, which designates the offspring as a component part of a kindred, as well as מנון, which, according as the מ is interpreted infin. or local, means either this, that it sprouts up luxuriantly, the abundant growth, or also the place of luxuriant sprouting, wanton growing, abundant and quick multiplication: thus the place of hatching, spawning. The subject in יהיה might be the fondled one; but it lies nearer, however, to take him who fondles as the subject, as in 21a. אחריתו is either adv. accus. for באחריתו, or, as we preferred at <reference osisRef="Prov.23.32">Pro 23:32</reference>, it is the subj. introducing, after the manner of a substantival clause, the following sentence as its virtual predicate: “one has fondled his servant from his youth up, and his (that of the one who fondles) end is: he will become a place of increase.” The master of the house is thought of along with his house; and the servant as one who, having become a man, presents his master with ילידי בּית, who are spoilt scapegraces, as he himself has become by the pampering of his master. There was used in the language of the people, נין for בּן, in the sense on which we name a degenerate son a “<hi type="italic">Schönes Früchtchen</hi>” [pretty little fruit]; and מנון is a place (house) where many נינים are; and a man (master of a house) who has many of them is one whose family has increased over his head. One reaches the same meaning if מנון is rendered more immediately as the place or state of growing, increasing, luxuriating. The sense is in any case: he will not be able, in the end, any more to defend himself against the crowd which grows up to him from this his darling, but will be merely a passive part of it.
entries.5131effafce8e54fd8341dcebc1b36b45eade1e1: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.22">Pro 29:22</reference> <div eID="gen11900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11901" type="x-p"/> The following group begins with a proverb which rhymes by מדון, with מנון of the foregoing, and extends on to the end of this Hezekiah collection: 22 A man of anger stirreth up strife;      And a passionate man aboundeth in transgression. <div eID="gen11901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11902" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of <reference osisRef="Prov.15.18">Pro 15:18</reference> and Pro 28:25. אישׁ and בּעל as here, but in the reverse order at Pro 22:24.<note placement="foot">For אישׁ־אף (Löwenstein after Norzi) is to be written, with Baer (<hi type="italic">Thorath Emeth</hi>, p. 19), אישׁ אף ,)91. Thus also in Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>.</note> אף here means anger, not the nose, viz., the expanded nostrils (Schultens). In רב־פּשׁע the פשׁע is, after <reference osisRef="Prov.14.29">Pro 14:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.16">Pro 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.27">Pro 20:27</reference>, the governed genitive; Hitzig construes it in the sense of פשׁע רב, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.2">Psa 19:2</reference>, with יגרה, but one does not say גּרה פשׁע; and that which is true of רבּים, that, after the manner of a numeral, it can precede its substantive (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Ps. 7:26; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.51">Psa 89:51</reference>), cannot be said of רב. Much (great) in wickedness denotes one who heaps up many wicked actions, and burdens himself with greater guilt (cf. פשׁע, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.16">Pro 29:16</reference>). The wrathful man stirreth up (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.15.18">Pro 15:18</reference>) strife, for he breaks through the mutual relations of men, which rest on mutual esteem and love, and by means of his passionate conduct he makes enemies of those against whom he thinks that he has reason for being angry; that on account of which he is angry can be settled without producing such hostility, but passion impels him on, and misrepresents the matter; it embitters hearts, and tears them asunder. The lxx has, instead of רב, ἐξώρυξεν, of dreaming, כרה (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.27">Pro 16:27</reference>).
entries.0fa41d13b94e6a93ca725e8a4f9e85399bad762e: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.23">Pro 29:23</reference> <div eID="gen11902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11903" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.23">Pro 29:23</reference> passes from anger to haughtiness: <div eID="gen11903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11904" type="x-p"/> A man’s pride will bring him low; <div eID="gen11904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11905" type="x-p"/> But the lowly attaineth to honour. <div eID="gen11905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11906" type="x-p"/> Thus we translate תּתמך כּבוד (Lat. <hi type="italic">honorem obtinet</hi>) in accord with <reference osisRef="Prov.11.16">Pro 11:16</reference>, and שׁפל־רוּח with <reference osisRef="Prov.16.19">Pro 16:19</reference>, where, however, שׁפל is not adj. as here, but inf. The haughty man obscures the honour which he has by this, that he boasts immeasurably of it, and aspires yet more after it; the lowly man, on the other hand, obtains honour without his seeking it, honour before God and before men, which would be of no worth were it not connected with the honour before God. The lxx: τοὺς δὲ ταπεινόφρονας ἐπείδει δόξῃ κύριους. This κύριους is indeed not contrary to the sense, but it is opposed to the style. Why the 24th verse should now follow is, as regards the contents and the expression, hard to say; but one observes that <reference osisRef="Prov.29.22-Prov.29.27">Pro 29:22-27</reference> follow each other, beginning with the successive letters of the alphabet א (ב), ג, ח, ח, ר, ת (ת).
entries.86058cb58ee3c37aa409296f05e0ff969ae88d6b: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.24">Pro 29:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.24">24</reference> He that taketh part with a thief hateth himself;      He heareth the oath and confesseth not. <div eID="gen11906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11907" type="x-p"/> Hitzig renders the first member as the pred. of the second: “he who does not bring to light such sins as require an atonement (Lev 5:1.), but shares the secret of them with the sinner, is not better than one who is a partner with a thief, who hateth himself.” The construction of the verse, he remarks, is not understood by any interpreter. It is not, however, so cross, - for, understood as Hitzig thinks it ought to be, the author should have expressed the subject by שׁמע אלה ולא יגיד, - but is simple as the order of the words and the verbal form require it. The oath is, after <reference osisRef="Lev.5.1">Lev 5:1</reference>, that of the judge who adjures the partner of the thief by God to tell the truth; but he conceals it, and burdens his soul with a crime worthy of death, for from a concealer he becomes in addition a perjured man.
entries.60d4e2124b9398f10d948f13786ea651d1616377: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">Pro 29:25</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">25</reference> Fear of man bringeth a snare with it;      But he that trusteth in Jahve is advanced. <div eID="gen11907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11908" type="x-p"/> It sounds strange, Hitzig remarks, that here in the Book of an Oriental author one should be warned against the fear of man. It is enough, in reply to this, to point to Isa 51:12. One of the two translations in the lxx (cf. Jerome and Luther) has found this “strange” thought not so strange as not to render it, and that in the gnomic aorist: φοβηθέντες καὶ αἰσχυνθέντες ἀνθρώπους ὑπεσκελίσθησαν. And why should not חרדּת אדם be able to mean the fear of man (cowardice)? Perhaps not so that אדם is the <hi type="italic">gen. objecti</hi>, but so that חרדת אדם means to frighten men, as in 1Sa 14:15. חרדת אלהים, a trembling of God; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.64.2">Psa 64:2</reference>; פחד איב, the fear occasioned by the enemy, although this connection, after <reference osisRef="Deut.2.25">Deu 2:25</reference>, can also mean fear of the enemy (<hi type="italic">gen. objecti</hi>). To יתּן, occasioned = brings as a consequence with it, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.10.10">Pro 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.13.15">Pro 13:15</reference>; the <hi type="italic">synallage generis</hi> is as at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.25">Pro 12:25</reference> : it is at least strange with fem. infinit. and infinitival nouns, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.16">Pro 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.14">Pro 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.28">Psa 73:28</reference>; but חרדּה (trembling) is such a <hi type="italic">nom. actionis</hi>, Ewald, §238a. Regarding ישׂגּב (for which the lxx.1 σωθήσεται, and lxx2 εὐφρανθήσεται = ישׂמח), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 18:10. He who is put into a terror by a danger with which men threaten him, so as to do from the fear of man what is wrong, and to conceal the truth, falls thereby into a snare laid by himself - it does not help him that by this means he has delivered himself from the danger, for he brands himself as a coward, and sins against God, and falls into an agony of conscience (reproach and anguish of heart) which is yet worse to bear than the evil wherewith he was threatened. It is only confidence in God that truly saves. The fear of man plunges him into yet greater suffering than that from which he would escape; confidence in God, on the other hand, lifts a man internally, and at last externally, above all his troubles.
entries.bdc8a8a9a2d7d307e72b2c67c1517c5b0da4d5f6: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.26">Pro 29:26</reference> <div eID="gen11908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11909" type="x-p"/> A similar gen. connection to that between חרדת אדם exists between משׁפט־אישׁ: <div eID="gen11909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11910" type="x-p"/> Many seek the countenance of the ruler; <div eID="gen11910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11911" type="x-p"/> Yet from Jahve cometh the judgment of men. <div eID="gen11911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11912" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of <reference osisRef="Prov.19.6">Pro 19:6</reference>, cf. 1Ki 10:24. It lies near to interpret אישׁ as <hi type="italic">gen. obj</hi>.: the judgment regarding any one, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the estimating of the man, the decision regarding him; and it is also possible, for משׁפּטי, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.2">Psa 17:2</reference>, may be understood of the judgment which I have, as well as of the judgment pronounced regarding me (cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">Lam 3:59</reference>). But the usage appears to think of the genit. after משׁפט always as subjective, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.33">Pro 16:33</reference>, of the decision which the lot brings, <reference osisRef="Job.36.6">Job 36:6</reference>, the right to which the poor have a claim; so that thus in the passage before us משׁפט־אשׁ means the right of a man, as that which is proper or fitting to him, the judgment of a man, as that to which as appropriate he has a claim (lxx τὸ δίκαιον ἀνδρί). Whether the genit. be rendered in the one way or the other, the meaning remains the same: it is not the ruler who finally decides the fate and determines the worth of a man, as they appear to think who with eye-service court his favour and fawn upon him.
entries.5ee137b68c84891236997cfa1e2ba658d5a6e868: <reference osisRef="Prov.29.27">Pro 29:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.29.27">27</reference> An abomination to a righteous man is a villanous man;      And an abomination to the godless is he who walketh uprightly. <div eID="gen11912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11913" type="x-p"/> In all the other proverbs which begin with תועבת, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.20">Pro 11:20</reference>, יהוה follows as genit., here צדּיקים, whose judgment is like that of God. אישׁ עול is an abhorrence to them, not as a man, but just as of such a character; עול is the direct contrast to ישׁר. The righteous sees in the villanous man, who boldly does that which is opposed to morality and to honour, an adversary of his God; on the other hand, the godless sees in the man that walketh uprightly (ישׁר־דּרך, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.37.14">Psa 37:14</reference>) his adversary, and the condemnation of himself. <div eID="gen11913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11914" type="x-p"/> With this doubled ת the Book of Proverbs, prepared by the men of Hezekiah, comes to an end. It closes, in accordance with its intention announced at the beginning, with a proverb concerning the king, and a proverb of the great moral contrasts which are found in all circles of society up to the very throne itself.  <chapter eID="Prov.29"/> <div eID="gen11914" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Seest thou a man <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> hasty <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> matters.</ns0:note> in his words <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>in his Business,</ns0:hi> who is rash and heady in the ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nagement of his affairs.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> more hope of a fool <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who is sensible of his folly, and willing to hearken to the advice of others, as this word is used<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Ch. 26. 12. though commonly it be meant of a wilful and wicked fool.</ns0:note>, than of him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he is self confident, and neither considers things seriously within himself, nor seeks counsel from the wise.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 He that delicately bringeth up his servant <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Allowing him too much freedom, and familiarity, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />licious fare.</ns0:note> from a child, shall have him become <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> son <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Will find him at last grow insolent and presump<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tuous and forgetful of his servile condition.</ns0:note> at the length.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 15. 18. & 26. 21.</ns0:note> An angry man stirreth up strife: and a furious man aboundeth in transgression <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Is by his passion easily transported into grievous and manifold sins, against God, and others, and himself, as swearing, and cursing, and violence, yea somtimes even to murder.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 22. 29. Ch. 15. 33. & 18. 12. Matt. 23. 12. Luk. 14. 11. & 18. 14. Jam. 4. 6, 10. 1 Pet. 5. 5.</ns0:note> A mans pride shall bring him low <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Because both God and Man conspire against him and abhor him.</ns0:note>: but ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour shall uphold the humble in spirit <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, as others render it, without any difference in the sense, <ns0:hi>the humble in Spirit shall hold</ns0:hi> their <ns0:hi>honour,</ns0:hi> shall be honoured by God and men. Thus honour, like a shadow, flees from them that pursue it, and follows them who flee from it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Whoso is partner with a thief <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By receiving a share of the stolen Goods upon condition of his concealment of the theft.</ns0:note>, hateth his own soul <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He carrieth himself towards it as if he hated it, he woundeth and destroyeth it.</ns0:note>: he heareth cursing <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He <ns0:hi>heareth the voice of swearing,</ns0:hi> as is said, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 5. 1. the Oath given to him by a Judge adjuring him and other suspected Persons to give infor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mation concerning it.</ns0:note>, and bewrayeth <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> not <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which he is bound to do both by vertue of his Oath and for the publick good, which ought to be preferred before all private contracts or friendships.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 The fear of man <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Inordinate fear of harm or mischief from men, which is fitly opposed to trust in God, because it comes from a distrust of God's Promise and Providence.</ns0:note> bringeth a snare <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Is an occasion of many sins, and of great danger, both of injuries from men, and of sore punishments from God.</ns0:note>: but who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so putteth his trust in the LORD <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Keeping God's way, and securely relying upon God to protect him from the designs and rage of wicked men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb,</ns0:hi> shall <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> set on high.</ns0:note> shall be safe.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 19. 6.</ns0:note> Many seek <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of a Ruler.</ns0:note> the rulers favour <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Men study to please and ingage their Rulers by their obliging carriage and humble Petitions and all other means, supposing that to be the only way to procure either right or favour from them, as they need or desire it.</ns0:note>, but every mans judgment <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The decision of his cause and the success of all his endeavours.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>cometh</ns0:hi> from the LORD <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Dependeth wholly upon God who ruleth and inclineth their Minds and Hearts as it pleaseth him, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 21. 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 An unjust man <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> an abomination to the just <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Because such men, as such, are hated by God, and haters of and Enemies unto God and all goodness, and publick Plagues to the Church and State in which they live, and therefore he who loves these must needs hate them, as true Friends hate those who are Enemies to their Friends.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:hi>he that is</ns0:hi> upright in the way, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> abomination to the wicked <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Of which see above on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 10.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
